prompt.context: Our client is a zoo that is thinking about acquiring a famous zebra from an African preserve. It's a huge investment, but they believe the new zebra would be a great contribution to their animal community.
prompt.question: You have been engaged to help decide whether this is a good idea. What would you consider when trying to help your client make this decision?

clarifying_info.q: How many people visit the zoo annually?
What is the expected attendance benefit from acquiring the zebra?
clarifying_info.a: Another zoo that acquired a similar zebra had an 8% increase in attendance.

clarifying_info.q: What are the ongoing annual costs?
clarifying_info.a: Annual maintenance (food, health costs, additional trainers): $90K per year.

clarifying_info.q: What discount rate should we use?
clarifying_info.a: Use a discount rate of 20%. Assume immediate costs are paid today, and annual costs and benefits are realized beginning next year and sustained into perpetuity.

exhibits.title: Market Research Findings
exhibits.shows: A table of possible attendance increase scenarios with associated probabilities and annual revenue figures, plus a summary of expected additional annual revenue and expected total annual revenue.

framework: Investment Valuation: Assess the upfront and ongoing costs of acquiring the zebra versus the incremental revenue benefits from increased zoo attendance
Breakeven Analysis: Determine the minimum attendance increase required for the NPV of the acquisition to be zero
Risk Assessment: Evaluate whether a proposed insurance contract to hedge downside attendance risk is financially attractive to the zoo
Proxy Benchmarking: Use attendance data from a comparable zoo acquisition as a baseline estimate for expected attendance uplift

questions.prompt: Calculate the NPV of the zebra acquisition using the 8% attendance increase proxy.
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify annual benefit as incremental revenue from increased attendance, subtract annual maintenance costs, apply a perpetuity formula at the discount rate, and subtract upfront costs. Should arrive at a positive NPV of approximately $155K, suggesting the acquisition is financially viable at the 8% increase assumption.

math.answer: NPV = $155,000 (positive; acquisition appears financially viable at 8% attendance increase)

questions.prompt: What is the breakeven attendance increase required for a zero NPV?
questions.guidance: Candidate should set NPV = 0 and solve for the required incremental revenue, then back out the implied attendance increase percentage. Breakeven is ~7.3%, meaning attendance must increase by at least 7.3% for the project to break even.

math.setup: Set NPV = 0: -$1,195,000 + (required_revenue - $90,000) / 0.20 = 0. Solve for required_revenue, then divide by total annual revenue ($4,500,000) to get the % increase.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, evaluate whether the insurance contract is a good deal for the zoo. The insurance pays the zoo to top up revenue to $250,000/year whenever attendance increases are 5% or less. The premium is 1% of total annual revenues.
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate the annual premium cost and compare it to the expected annual benefit from the insurance (probability-weighted payout). The annual cost exceeds the expected benefit, so the insurance is not a good deal. Strong candidates will also note: (1) if attendance always exceeds 5%, the zoo pays premiums with zero benefit; (2) the contract functions like an option, and a different structure might be more suitable.

math.setup: Annual premium cost = 1% of expected total annual revenue = 0.01 x $4,752,000. Expected benefit = probability-weighted insurance payout at each scenario where attendance <= 5%. At 3% increase (revenue $135K, probability 20%): payout = $250K - $135K = $115K. At 5% increase (revenue $225K, probability 40%): payout = $250K - $225K = $25K. At 7% and 9% (revenue > $250K): payout = $0.
math.answer: Annual cost ($47,520) > Expected benefit ($33,000); the insurance is NOT a good deal for the zoo.

brainstorming.prompt: What additional considerations or next steps might the zoo explore to make the zebra acquisition more attractive?

categories.name: Negotiation
ideas: Negotiate a lower acquisition price for the zebra
Negotiate lower transportation or facility construction costs
Negotiate with the insurance company to increase the revenue guarantee threshold or reduce the premium

categories.name: Revenue Enhancement
ideas: Introduce a premium zebra exhibit ticket or add-on fee
Develop ancillary revenue streams (merchandise, educational programs, sponsorships tied to the zebra)
Use the zebra as a marketing hook to drive broader zoo membership growth

categories.name: Cost Reduction
ideas: Explore shared facilities with other animals to reduce capital outlay
Optimize staffing by cross-training existing trainers rather than hiring dedicated new ones

categories.name: Risk Mitigation
ideas: Commission a more granular market research study before committing
Negotiate a conditional purchase agreement or trial loan of the zebra before full acquisition
Explore whether another zoo would co-fund the acquisition to share risk and cost

recommendation: Based on the market research, it is unlikely that the zebra acquisition is a good idea. The breakeven attendance increase required is 7.3%, but the market research suggests a weighted-average attendance increase of only ~5.6%, making it improbable the zoo will break even on the investment.
The insurance contract offered does not create value for the zoo: annual premium cost ($47,520) exceeds the expected annual benefit ($33,000).
risks: Attendance increase may be lower than the 8% proxy from the comparable zoo, consistent with market research findings
The insurance contract costs more than the expected benefit it provides
If attendance never exceeds 5%, the zoo pays premiums indefinitely with no offset
next_steps: Negotiate with the insurance company to restructure the contract — either reduce the premium or increase the revenue guarantee — to make it value-accretive
Explore alternative revenue-enhancement strategies (premium ticketing, sponsorship) to reduce reliance on attendance growth alone
Consider commissioning additional market research to narrow the probability distribution of attendance outcomes before making a final acquisition decision
